481.quote_or_event: “This mendicant who knows the time, the strength (of himself), the measure (of all things), the practice, the occasion (for begging, &c.), the conduct, the religious precepts, the true condition (of the donor or hearer), … he proceeds securely (on the road to final liberation) after having cut off both (love and hate).”
481.explanation: The Acaranga describes the wise mendicant as one who knows the right time, his own strength and the occasion, and who therefore moves securely toward liberation.
481.tie_back: Valluvar's crow beats the owl because it knows its hour; the Acaranga likewise pairs knowing the time with knowing one's own strength as the mark of the wise, though its goal is liberation rather than victory.
481.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.5.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
481._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (ellipsis marks omitted clauses). Strong match on knowing time and strength together; the context is monastic begging, not contest with an enemy.

482.quote_or_event: “At the right time a monk should sally forth, and he should return at the right time; avoiding to do anything out of time, he should do what is appropriate for each period of the day.”
482.explanation: The opening lecture on discipline makes timeliness a rule of the monk's whole day: each act has its proper hour and nothing is to be done out of season.
482.tie_back: The kural says acting in step with the season binds Fortune; this verse shares the principle of doing each thing at its fitting time, though for a Jain monk the reward is discipline, not wealth.
482.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
482._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close on acting in season; the image of Fortune (Tirumakal) tied by a rope has no Jain counterpart, and Jainism does not seek worldly fortune.

483.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra opens by declaring that right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together form the path to liberation. Jain teaching holds that a soul fit for liberation who takes up these three means will in time reach even that hardest of goals.
483.explanation: Jainism names the specific means (the three jewels) by which the most difficult of all undertakings, freeing the soul from karma, is accomplished.
483.tie_back: The kural asks whether anything is impossible for one who acts with the right means at the right time; Jainism answers similarly about liberation, given the proper means applied over time.
483.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.1 of Umasvati (paraphrase of the sutra's content)
483._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known sutra, not quoted. The parallel is structural only: the kural concerns a king's resources and timing, while the sutra concerns spiritual means.

484.quote_or_event: In Hemacandra's account of the first universal monarch, Bharata, son of Rishabhanatha, sets out on his conquest of the six divisions of Bharatavarsha only after the discus-jewel (cakra-ratna) appears in his armoury, and by a long, staged campaign brings the whole land under his rule. Jain tradition then shows him renouncing it all and attaining omniscience.
484.explanation: The Jain Puranic tradition does contain a world-conquest that succeeds when the sign of the right moment has appeared, but it treats such dominion as worldly and ultimately to be given up.
484.tie_back: The kural promises that even the whole world comes within reach if time and place are rightly chosen; Bharata's digvijaya is the Jain example of exactly such a conquest, though Jainism values his later renunciation more highly.
484.source: Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra of Hemacandra, Book 1, Bharata's conquest (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; paraphrase)
484._accuracy_note: Paraphrased narrative; wording and chapter divisions not checked against Johnson's text in this session. Jainism sees conquest as binding karma, so the fit is to the event, not to the value placed on it.

485.quote_or_event: “A restrained, very learned, and wise (monk) should accept such alms as are freely given him, being free from passions and waiting for his end. This is the doctrine of the Kêvalin.”
485.explanation: The Path lecture closes by describing the sage who lives free of passion and calmly waits for his appointed end.
485.tie_back: The kural praises those who wait undisturbed for their time; the Jain sage also waits calmly and without agitation, though what he awaits is the end of life and liberation, not the chance to win the world.
485.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
485._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The shared element is calm, unshaken waiting; the object waited for is entirely different, so this is a next-best match.

486.quote_or_event: When Bahubali, after defeating his elder brother Bharata in the contests that settled their war, raised his fist for a final blow, he stopped, judged that striking his brother would be wrong, and turned the same raised hand on himself, pulling out his hair in the ascetic's renunciation. Jain tradition then shows him standing in unmoving meditation until he gained omniscience.
486.explanation: The story turns a blow held back into a greater victory: the energy withdrawn from striking an outward foe is redirected against the passions within.
486.tie_back: The kural's ram draws back so that it can strike harder; Bahubali's drawn-back fist also becomes a stronger blow, aimed at his own karma rather than at an enemy.
486.source: Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra of Hemacandra, Book 1, Bharata and Bahubali (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; paraphrase)
486._accuracy_note: Well-known Jain narrative, paraphrased; exact wording and chapter not verified against Johnson in this session. The parallel of a held-back blow is close, but the Jain point is renouncing combat, not timing it.

487.quote_or_event: “He should not speak unasked, and asked he should not tell a lie; he should not give way to his anger, and bear with indifference pleasant and unpleasant occurrences.”
487.explanation: The monk is told not to give way to anger at all and to meet both pleasant and unpleasant events with equanimity.
487.tie_back: The kural's wise man hides his anger and waits for the right time; Jainism agrees that anger should not burst out, but it asks for anger to be given up rather than stored for later.
487.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
487._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It agrees only on outward restraint. The kural's idea of seething inwardly while waiting conflicts with the Jain aim of removing anger (krodha), one of the four passions.

488.quote_or_event: “There is not the least hatred in me, neither now, nor before, nor in future. The Yakshas attend upon me, therefore they have beaten the boys.”
488.explanation: The beaten monk Harikesa bears abuse and blows without hatred, and his attackers are nevertheless brought low, not by him but by the guardian spirits.
488.tie_back: The kural advises bearing one's foes until their time of downfall comes; in this story the monk too bears his enemies and they fall, but Jainism insists that he wanted no revenge at all.
488.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
488._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Partial match on enduring enemies who later fall; the strategic patience aimed at the enemy's ruin in the kural is opposed to Jain non-hatred.

489.quote_or_event: “A rare chance, in the long course of time, is human birth for a living being; hard are the consequences of actions; Gautama, be careful all the while!”
489.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that human birth is a rare opportunity across vast ages and must be used without a moment's carelessness.
489.tie_back: The kural urges seizing a rare opportunity at once to do what would otherwise be impossible; Jainism makes the same demand about the rarest opportunity of all, a human life in which liberation can be pursued.
489.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.4 (refrain from 10.1) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
489._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (the refrain is abbreviated '&c.' in 10.4 and given in full in 10.1). Strong fit on seizing a rare chance; it is applied to spiritual effort rather than worldly action.

490.quote_or_event: “As dhaṅkas, herons, ospreys, cormorants, and pheasants meditate upon capturing fish, (which is) a sinful and very low meditation, so some heretical, unworthy Sramanas contemplate the pursuit of pleasures; (they are) sinful and very low like herons.”
490.explanation: The Sutrakritanga uses the heron's still, fish-watching posture as an image of false meditation, a show of stillness that hides a predatory aim.
490.tie_back: Valluvar praises the heron's stillness before it strikes as a model of good timing; the Jain text uses the same bird for the opposite lesson, so it is an honest contrast rather than an agreement.
490.source: Sutrakritanga I.11.27-28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
490._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Same image but opposite judgment; Jain ahimsa cannot praise the heron's strike, so this is a contrast, not a match.
